newsitem.title: USA: Calif. drops phased-in retail power market plan.
newsitem.headline: Calif. drops phased-in retail power market plan.

text.p: California's Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) at a meeting here on Tuesday dropped a proposal to phase in open competition among power suppliers in the state's retail electricity market.
The move leaves in place, with some modifications, an earlier proposal to open the state's entire retail electricity market to competition from January 1, 1998.
The move puts the nation's most populous state firmly in the vanguard of the trend toward lower electricity rates by allowing customers to choose their power supplier.

At the meeting, CPUC president Gregory Conlon withdrew his proposal to initially limit open competition to a pool of users whose demand would not exceed 1,800 megawatts (MW), or about five percent of peak usage in California.
But his decision was contingent on the commission accepting two modifications to the original plan for full open competition from New Year.
One of the changes will require utilities to report to the CPUC in July how many direct access transactions they will be able to process as of Januray 1.
The other change lowers the threshold for customers allowed to participate in direct access through real-time metering to 20 kilowatts (kw) from the previously proposed 50 kw.
Smaller customers may participate in direct access through "load profiling", with billing determined by typical time-of-use patterns.

This billing system will calibrate electricity bills according to the hour of the day the power is used, with power used during peak demand hours commanding a higher price than power used during off-peak hours.
The CPUC decision also allows aggregation of smaller customers by power suppliers.
The CPUC also ruled anyone planning to offer electrical services to California customers will be required to register with the Commission starting in July.

In a separate decision at today's meeting, the CPUC said it will allow companies other than utilities to compete in the state to supply customers with electricity services such as metering and billing.
Distribution utilities will be required to identify any cost-savings from third-party service providers and return those savings to customers.
This ruling was strongly opposed by the state's biggest investor-owned utilities, especially Edison International, the parent of Southern California Edison Co (SoCal Edison).
SoCal Edison serves most of southern California except Los Angles and the San Diego area.
Jessie Knight, the commissioner assigned to the electricity restructring proceeding, said today's decision was "a blueprint for other states since in many ways California is at the forefront."

The federal government, through the Federal Energy Regulatory Commisssion in Washington, has instructed the nation's power industry to deregulate, but is leaving the details of implementing this mandate to each state.
